prompt: What is the shape of a middleware in Go's standard library style?
hint: It takes the handler to wrap.

choices.text: A type that embeds `http.ServeMux` and overrides its routing method
choices.why: No framework type is involved; a function from handler to handler is the whole idea.

choices.text: An interface `Middleware` from `net/http`
choices.why: `net/http` declares no such interface.

choices.text: `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) error`
choices.why: That is a handler that returns an error, a shape some frameworks use; it wraps nothing.

choices.text: `func(next http.Handler) http.Handler`
choices.why: Right. It receives `next` and returns a handler that decides when to call it.

prompt: In `wrap`, `h = announce("inner")(h)` runs before `h = announce("outer")(h)`. Which line does the server print first for a request?
hint: Which wrapper did the server receive?

choices.text: `outer in`
choices.why: Right. The last wrapper applied is outermost, so it runs first and finishes last.

choices.text: `inner in`
choices.why: `inner` was applied first, so it ended up inside `outer`.

choices.text: `  the handler`, since middlewares print after the handler
choices.why: Each middleware prints before calling `next` as well as after.

choices.text: It varies between requests, because each one runs in its own goroutine
choices.why: Inside one request the calls are nested and ordered, like a call stack.

prompt: `curl localhost:8080/nothing` gets a 404 from `wrap`. What did the two middlewares print for it?
hint: Look at the second half of the server's output.

choices.text: Their in and out lines, around the mux's 404
choices.why: Right. A middleware wraps whatever is inside it, answers nobody wrote included.

choices.text: Nothing, because no route matched
choices.why: They wrap the whole mux, including its 404.

choices.text: Only `outer in` and `outer out`
choices.why: `inner` wraps the mux too, so it ran as well.

choices.text: A panic, because `next` is nil when nothing matches the path
choices.why: `next` is the mux, which answers 404 itself.

prompt: `chain(mux, a, b)` builds the same handler as `a(___(mux))`.
hint: The first middleware named is outermost.

prompt: Why does `logRequests` pass the handler a `statusRecorder` instead of the real writer?
hint: What is missing from `ResponseWriter`?

choices.text: A writer has no method to read back the status
choices.why: Right. The recorder notes the code as it passes, so the middleware knows it afterwards.

choices.text: To stop handlers from writing headers
choices.why: Everything passes through to the real writer; nothing is stopped.

choices.text: To buffer the body so that the log line is written before the response leaves
choices.why: Nothing is buffered; the line is written after the handler returns.

choices.text: Because a real `ResponseWriter` is not safe to use from a middleware goroutine
choices.why: Middleware and handler run in the same goroutine, one calling the other.

prompt: A handler writes a body and never calls `WriteHeader`. What status does `statusRecorder` record?
hint: What will the real writer send?

choices.why: `Write` sets 200 when no status came before it.

choices.text: 204, since no status was chosen
choices.why: 204 means no content, and there was a body.

choices.text: Whatever the handler would have chosen if it had called `WriteHeader` before its first write
choices.why: Nothing guesses intentions: the first write sends 200.
Right. A write with no status first means 200, and the recorder notes exactly that.

prompt: What would be lost if `statusRecorder` had no `Unwrap` method?
hint: A wrapper hides the methods its type does not declare.

choices.text: Flushing through `http.ResponseController`
choices.why: Right. `Unwrap` is the convention it follows to dig through wrappers, and lesson 13 needs it.

choices.text: Nothing; embedding already exposes every method of the real writer
choices.why: Embedding exposes the interface's three methods, not the extra ones the real writer has, like flushing.

choices.text: The byte count, since `Write` would go straight to the real writer
choices.why: `Write` counts the bytes; `Unwrap` plays no part in it.

choices.text: The log line's duration
choices.why: The middleware's clock measures that.

prompt: In the log, how many bytes did boxoffice send for `GET /events/9`?
hint: The number before the `B`.

prompt: Why does the access log hold the path but not the query string or the headers?
hint: Who reads a log, and for how long is it kept?

choices.text: Secrets would leak into it
choices.why: Right. A token in `Authorization` or an address in a query string would sit in a file many people read for a long time.

choices.text: Headers are not available after the handler returns
choices.why: `r.Header` is still there; leaving it out is a choice.

choices.text: A query string is too long for `log.Printf`
choices.why: Length is not the reason; what it holds is.

choices.text: The mux strips them before middleware sees the request
choices.why: The logger sits outside the mux and sees the request as it arrived.

prompt: Against `fragile`, which exit status did `curl` report for `/boom`?
hint: curl's code for an empty reply.

prompt: With no recovery middleware, what does `net/http` do when a handler panics?
hint: Did `fragile` keep running?

choices.text: Logs, closes the connection, serves on
choices.why: Right. The process survives; the client is left with an empty reply.

choices.text: The whole program exits with status 2
choices.why: That is a panic outside a request; `net/http` recovers handler panics.

choices.text: It sends a 500 with the panic message in the body
choices.why: The client got no status at all, which is why curl said 52.

choices.text: It runs the handler a second time, in case the panic came from a passing condition
choices.why: Nothing is retried; a retry of a bug is the same bug.

prompt: Reading the stack `fragile` printed, where is the line that caused the panic?
hint: Read from the top down.

choices.text: The last line, where `net/http.(*Server).Serve` created the goroutine
choices.why: That is where the goroutine began, far from the bug.

choices.text: In `runtime/panic.go`
choices.why: That is the runtime reporting the panic.

choices.text: At `main.main.func1`, `main.go:13`
choices.why: Right. The first frame of your own code is the line that wrote to the nil map.

choices.text: At the top, in `net/http.(*conn).serve.func1`
choices.why: That is the recovering code inside `net/http`.

prompt: A handler starts a goroutine, and that goroutine panics. What does `recoverPanics` do about it?
hint: Where does `recover` work?

choices.text: It turns it into a 500 like any other panic
choices.why: `recover` only sees panics of its own goroutine.

choices.text: It logs the stack and lets the goroutine continue
choices.why: It never sees the panic, and a panicking goroutine does not continue.

choices.text: Nothing, and the whole program ends
choices.why: Right. A goroutine started by a handler has to protect itself.

choices.text: `net/http` recovers it and closes the client's connection
choices.why: `net/http` only recovers the goroutine it runs the handler in.

prompt: Why does `recoverPanics` panic again when the value is `http.ErrAbortHandler`?
hint: Who panics with that value, and why?

choices.text: Because `recover` returns nil for it
choices.why: It returns the value; that is how the middleware recognises it.

choices.text: To crash the program so a supervisor restarts it
choices.why: `net/http` catches it in the connection's goroutine; the program goes on.

choices.text: It marks a deliberate abort
choices.why: Right. A 500 would undo the deliberate abort.

choices.text: Since it marks a client that disconnected
choices.why: A disconnected client cancels the context; this value is a handler's own choice.

prompt: `curl -H 'Origin: https://elsewhere.example.net' localhost:8080/events/1` got a 200 with the whole body. What does that show?
hint: Who enforces CORS?

choices.text: The cors middleware is broken
choices.why: It did its job: no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for that origin.

choices.text: CORS is not access control
choices.why: Right. Anything private needs authentication.

choices.text: curl ignores the Origin header
choices.why: It sent it; the server read it.

choices.text: Unknown origins are allowed to read every `GET` answer by default
choices.why: No permission header was sent for it.

prompt: Why does `cors` add `Vary: Origin` to every answer, allowed or not?
hint: Think of a cache between client and server.

choices.text: Browsers refuse responses without it
choices.why: They accept them; the danger is in caches.

choices.text: It tells the browser which origins are allowed to read the answer
choices.why: That is `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.

choices.text: The answer depends on a request header, so a cache must not reuse one origin's copy for another
choices.why: Right. Without it a CDN or the browser's cache might serve the wrong permission.

choices.text: It speeds up the preflight
choices.why: `Access-Control-Max-Age` does that.

prompt: Match each header in the preflight answer to what it tells the browser.
hint: Four headers, four permissions.

pairs.right: which page may read the answer
which methods the real request may use
which request headers it may carry
how long to remember this answer

right_distractors: which token the request must send

prompt: How many seconds may a browser remember boxoffice's preflight answer?
hint: `Access-Control-Max-Age`.

prompt: Why must `cors` answer the preflight before `requireStaff` is reached?
hint: What does a browser put in a preflight?

choices.text: `requireStaff` is slower than `cors`
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: A browser sends it with no token
choices.why: Right. The real request would never be sent.

choices.text: `OPTIONS` requests skip middleware
choices.why: They go through every middleware like any other request.

choices.text: The admin mux answers `OPTIONS` with the report
choices.why: Only `GET /admin/report` is registered there.

prompt: Match each request to `/admin/report` to the status it got.
hint: Who is calling, and may they?

prompt: What is the difference between the 401 and the 403 boxoffice sends?
hint: Authentication against authorisation.

choices.text: 401: unknown caller; 403: known caller, not allowed
choices.why: Right. The door token is real, so its answer is 403.

choices.text: 401 is for a wrong password, 403 for a missing header
choices.why: Both of those are unknown callers, and both got 401.

choices.text: 403 comes from the middleware and 401 from the handler
choices.why: The other way round: the middleware sends 401, `salesReport` sends 403.

choices.text: None in practice; clients treat them the same
choices.why: One asks for credentials, the other says credentials will not help.

prompt: Why does `requireStaff` compare tokens with `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare` rather than `==`?
hint: Where does `==` stop?

choices.text: `==` does not work on strings read from headers
choices.why: It works; it leaks time.

choices.text: It is faster for long tokens
choices.why: Speed is not the point; equal time is.

choices.text: `==` takes longer the more of a guess is right
choices.why: Right. Measured over a network, that guides guessing one character at a time.

choices.text: To accept tokens that differ only in case
choices.why: It compares bytes exactly.

prompt: Why is the context key `roleKey{}`, an unexported struct type, and not the string `"role"`?
hint: Who else puts values into a request's context?

choices.text: Strings are not allowed as context keys
choices.why: They are allowed, and that is the danger.

choices.text: An empty struct makes the lookup faster than a string
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; collisions are.

choices.text: Because `context.WithValue` panics on a string key
choices.why: It accepts one; vet tools warn about it.

choices.text: No other package names that type, so none reads or overwrites the value by accident
choices.why: Right. `staffRole` is the only way in.

prompt: Why does boxoffice read the tokens from environment variables rather than from a command-line flag?
hint: What does `ps` show?

choices.text: Flags are limited to 16 characters
choices.why: No such limit exists.

choices.text: The `flag` package cannot parse hex
choices.why: A token is read as a string either way.

choices.text: `ps` shows command lines to everyone
choices.why: Right. A secret in a flag is a secret on display.

choices.text: Environment variables are encrypted by the kernel
choices.why: They are not; they only stay off the command line.

prompt: Why is `logRequests` the outermost middleware in boxoffice?
hint: What must the log see?

choices.text: It is the cheapest, so it goes first
choices.why: Cost is not the argument; what it sees is.

choices.text: `chain` requires a logger first
choices.why: `chain` takes any middlewares in any order.

choices.text: It must see every final answer: the 500 from `recoverPanics` and the 204 from `cors`
choices.why: Right. Anything outside it would answer without a log line.

choices.text: A panic inside it would otherwise crash the server
choices.why: `net/http` recovers handler panics anyway; the order is about the log line.

prompt: A new route `GET /admin/refunds` is added to the `admin` mux next month. What protects it?
hint: Where is `requireStaff` applied?

choices.text: The token check on the `/admin/` subtree
choices.why: Right. Every path under `/admin/` passes `requireStaff` before the inner mux sees it.

choices.text: Nothing, until someone wraps the new handler
choices.why: The check sits on the subtree, not on each handler.

choices.text: CORS, because it names one origin
choices.why: CORS protects nothing on the server.

choices.text: `recoverPanics`
choices.why: It turns panics into 500s; it checks nobody.

prompt: `go run .` prints `no staff tokens: set BOXOFFICE_MANAGER_TOKEN` and exits. Why does boxoffice refuse to start?
hint: What would the staff routes be without a token?

choices.text: Port 8080 is taken
choices.why: That message is `address already in use`.

choices.text: The door token is required as well as the manager's, and it was missing
choices.why: Either token is enough; the loop keeps whichever is set.

choices.text: `go vet` failed
choices.why: `go vet` printed nothing.

choices.text: No token is set at all
choices.why: Right. Better a refusal now than a 401 to puzzle over later.

prompt: Put the code a staff request to `/admin/report` passes through in order, from the server to the handler.
hint: `chain` puts the first middleware outermost.
trap: `requireStaff` sits behind the main mux, on the subtree only.

prompt: Someone swaps the order to `chain(mux, recoverPanics, logRequests, cors(...))`. A handler panics. What changes?
hint: The panic unwinds through `logRequests` before reaching `recover`.

choices.text: The client gets an empty reply instead of a 500
choices.why: `recoverPanics` is still there and still sends the 500.

choices.text: Nothing; the order of middlewares is a matter of taste
choices.why: The table in section 07 argues each position.

choices.text: The panic is logged twice
choices.why: `recoverPanics` logs it once; the access line is the one lost.

choices.text: The request gets no log line, because the panic skips the code after `next.ServeHTTP` in the logger
choices.why: Right. The 500 still goes out, and nobody records it.
